Inside one server
An NVIDIA DGX H100: the standard building block of an AI cluster
  • 8 × NVIDIA H100 GPUs do the math. Each has 80 GB of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) right beside it.
  • NVLink switches join every GPU to every other at 900 GB/s, so the 8 act like one.
  • 2 × Intel Xeon 8480C CPUs (56 cores each, 2 TB of memory) run the system, feed in data and schedule work.
  • NVMe flash (about 30 TB): training data and checkpoints while training; model weights and cached prompts while serving.
  • 8 × 400 Gb/s network cards link it to the rest of the cluster.

Large models are mostly matrix math
Every layer multiplies a matrix of numbers by a matrix of learned weights
One blue output = one row × one column, multiplied pair by pair and added up. In Kimi K2 that is 7,168 multiply-adds.
  • Attention: matrix multiplies turn each word into queries, keys and values, then mix them.
  • Feed-forward experts: more matrix multiplies, in every layer.
  • The rest (softmax, activations, normalization) is a sliver.
~74 billionmath operations for every word Kimi K2 writes (with a 4,096-word context)
99.9%of them are matrix multiplications: the same simple operation, repeated billions of times
Running a model is multiplying huge matrices, over and over, so the question is which chip does that best.
Source: Moonshot AI, Kimi K2 model card, 2025 (hidden size 7,168; 61 layers; 64 attention heads; 32B active parameters). Operation count and 99.9% share: our estimate at a 4,096-token context (2 operations per active weight plus attention; non-matrix work counted at ~5 operations per value).
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
GPUs are efficient and fast at math
NVIDIA H100 vs. Intel Xeon 8480C, the CPU that sits beside it in the same server
CPU: a few big cores
GPU: thousands of small units
H100 GPUXeon 8480C CPU
Power700 W350 W
Parallel FP32 lanes16,8961,792
Peak math, FP3267 TFLOPS7.2 TFLOPS
Peak math, BF16 tensor cores989 TFLOPS—
Memory bandwidth3,350 GB/s307 GB/s
  • Power ≈ switches per second × energy per switch. Each transistor that flips charges a tiny capacitor, and that energy ends up as heat.
  • This CPU spends its transistors on making one thread fast: branch prediction, reordering, big caches. Most are idle in any given cycle.
  • This GPU spends them on arithmetic and keeps thousands of units busy every cycle.
  • Per operation, the GPU is more efficient: 4.7× more math per joule in FP32, 69× with its tensor cores. It draws more because it does 9× to 138× more math every second.
A GPU isn't wasteful, it's busy: more operations every second, packed 8 to a server and 72 to a rack.
Sources: NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet (SXM: 700 W, 16,896 FP32 cores, 67 TFLOPS FP32, 989 TFLOPS dense BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Intel Xeon 8480 (56 cores, 2.0 GHz base, 350 W, 8 × DDR5-4800). CPU FP32 peak is our calculation: 56 cores × 2.0 GHz × 64 FLOPs per cycle (AVX-512); its AMX matrix units are not counted.

From chip to campus
An AI data center is the same few parts, nested five levels deep
  • GPU: does the math. The common one is the NVIDIA H100, about $25,000–40,000 new, or about $3.50–4.30 an hour to rent.
  • Server: 8 GPUs, 2 CPUs, memory, flash and network cards in one box: about $300,000–400,000.
  • Rack: a cabinet of servers sharing power and cooling. One NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack holds 72 GPUs and draws about 120–132 kW.
  • Cluster: thousands of racks wired into one network so they work as one computer.
  • Data center / campus: one or more buildings with power and cooling plants, sized in megawatts to gigawatts.

Not every rack is a GPU rack
A data hall seen from above: GPU, CPU and storage racks share one network
  • GPU racks train and serve models. About 120–132 kW each, so they must be liquid cooled.
  • CPU racks run the ordinary cloud: websites, databases, email. The average rack in the industry draws under 8 kW and is air cooled.
  • Storage racks hold flash and disks: data sets, model checkpoints, everyone's files.
  • The network links every server to every other, so a job can spread across the hall.

A GPU runs these operations trillions of times a second. What causes its power draw?
■ doing math ■ moving data
  • Moving data costs far more than math. One read from off-chip memory ≈ 170× a 32-bit multiply.
  • It's all transistors switching; a longer wire is more charge to move, so distance is what costs.
  • Caching reuses each number, so training spends mostly on math. Serving one user at a time is memory-bound; the fix is batching.
It's all switching; distance makes it expensive. Good chips and good software keep numbers close to the math.
Source: M. Horowitz, “Computing's energy problem (and what we can do about it),” ISSCC 2014 (45 nm), as tabulated in S. Han et al., “Learning both weights and connections for efficient neural networks,” NeurIPS 2015. 170× = 640 pJ ÷ 3.7 pJ.

How data centers get rid of heat
A power plant cools its steam; a data center cools its chips. Two steps, each trading power for water
1
Off the chips
AirFans push cool air through the servers; hot and cold aisles kept apart. Fine for CPU racks.
Rear-door coilA liquid coil on the back of an air-cooled rack catches the hot exhaust. A retrofit for denser racks.
Direct-to-chip liquidCold plates on each GPU and CPU, in a closed loop. What 130 kW GPU racks need.
ImmersionWhole servers sit in a tank of non-conducting fluid; no server fans. Still uncommon.
2
Out of the building
ChillersRefrigeration, like a giant air conditioner. Most electricity.
Free coolingCold outside air or water does the work; chillers rest. Needs a cool climate.
Evaporative towerEvaporating water carries heat off. Little electricity, uses water.
Dry coolerFans blow heat into the air. No water, more electricity on hot days.
Sea or lake waterLike a power plant's once-through cooling: cold water in, heat out.
Why Google runs at a PUE of 1.09
83% lessoverhead than the industry average: 0.09 vs. 0.54 per unit of computing (2025)
40% lesscooling energy when DeepMind's AI tuned the pumps, chillers and towers (2016)
SeawaterHamina, Finland, cools with the Gulf of Finland through heat exchangers, mixing the warm water before it goes back
Cooling is a menu, not a fixed cost: site, climate and design decide how much power and water it takes.
Sources: Data Center Frontier, “Tech explainer: data center cooling,” July 20, 2026 (methods and trade-offs). Google, data center efficiency page (fleet PUE 1.09 vs. 1.54 industry average, Uptime Institute 2025). DeepMind, “DeepMind AI reduces Google data centre cooling bill by 40%,” 2016. DCD, “Google's Finland data center pioneers new seawater cooling.”

Where the water goes
Water is used for cooling twice: the power plant cools its steam, and the data center cools its chips

Wind, solar, hydro

Once-through cooling evaporates less but withdraws far more: ~170 L per kWh pulled from a river or lake for nuclear, most of it returned warmer.
A · Cooling tower (open loop)Evaporates water to dump heat: about 1.9 L per kWh on average; ~80% of the water drawn in is lost to the air.
B · Dry cooler (closed loop)Fans blow the heat into the air: almost no water, more electricity on hot days. Microsoft says this avoids 125+ million L a year per site.
For scale, a 100 MW site for one day: ~4.6 million L evaporated on site with towers (A), plus ~6.1 million L at a nuclear plant with towers, or ~0 L from wind.
On site, water is a design choice; off site, it's a grid choice. Towers save power, dry coolers save water.
Sources: Macknick et al., “Operational water consumption and withdrawal factors for electricity generating technologies,” Environ. Res. Lett. 7, 045802 (2012), NREL (gal/MWh, converted). EESI, “Data centers and water consumption,” 2025 (average WUE 1.9 L/kWh; ~80% evaporates). Microsoft, “Sustainable by design: next-generation datacenters consume zero water for cooling,” Dec. 9, 2024. 100 MW example: our calculation.

Training vs. inference
The same chips do two very different jobs
Training: build the model once
  • Weeks of work on tens of thousands of GPUs, all in lockstep.
  • Every GPU waits for the slowest one, so it needs one site and a very fast network.
  • Done once per model, then again for the next model.
Inference: use the model, every time anyone asks
  • Millions of small, independent requests.
  • Can be spread over many sites, closer to the users.
  • Grows with every user, every day the model is in service.
  • Judged per answer: time to first word, words per second.
Training is one huge synchronized job; inference is millions of small ones. Next: how to make the small ones cheaper.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Cheaper inference: batching
Every new word needs every weight read from memory. Make each read do more work.
Batch of 1
Weights in memory
read once per word
Math units
0.3% busy
1 user
~161 pJ per operation: almost all of it spent fetching the weight
Batch of 256
Weights in memory
the same one read
Math units
87% busy
~1.4 pJ per operation: one fetch now feeds 256 users' math
Why we want the GPU fullFetching a number from memory costs far more than the math done with it, and an idle GPU still has to be paid for and powered. Fewer fetches per operation means less energy per operation and more answers per second from the same chip.
Math units busy (H100, writing text)
Energy per operation (picojoules, log scale)
A full GPU is an efficient GPU: ~150× less energy per operation at batch 512 than at batch 1.
Sources: NVIDIA H100 datasheet (989 TFLOPS dense BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Energy: Horowitz, ISSCC 2014 (45 nm): 640 pJ per 32-bit DRAM read, 1.5 pJ per 16-bit multiply-add; newer chips are lower, the ratio is what matters. Our calculation: energy per op = 320 pJ ÷ (2 × batch) + 0.75 pJ; ignores attention and KV-cache reads.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Cheaper inference: caching
Keep the results of old calculations and reuse them, so each new word only adds its own math
Without a cache
With a KV cache
■ recomputed ■ read from the cache ■ new work · a 4-word prompt, then 6 new words
Prompt caching goes one step further: a shared beginning (a system prompt, a long document) is processed once and reused by every request that starts with it.
1,000-word prompt, 1,000-word answer750× less work1,500,500 token passes without a cache vs. 2,000 with one
The price: memory, for every user, all the time9.2 GBKimi K2 keeps ~70 KB per token in FP16, so one 128k-token conversation fills 9.2 GB of GPU memory
Caching reuses old calculations, so there is far less work to do; the price is memory.
Source: Moonshot AI, Kimi K2 model card, 2025 (61 layers, multi-head latent attention as in DeepSeek-V3: 512 latent + 64 position dimensions per layer). Our calculations: KV size = (512 + 64) × 2 bytes (FP16) × 61 layers = 70,272 bytes per token; token passes = 1,001 + 1,002 + … + 2,000 = 1,500,500.

Smaller models, 2: distillation
A different, much smaller model, trained to imitate a big one
Teacher
DeepSeek-R1
671B weights,
37B used per word
“The capital of France is …” (illustrative)
Student
R1-Distill-Qwen-7B
7B weights
~5× less mathper word: 37B → 7B weights used
~96× less memoryto hold the model: 671B → 7B weights
  • Two ways to imitate: match the teacher's probabilities for every next word (more signal than a single right answer), or train on answers the teacher writes. DeepSeek made its distilled models the second way, from about 800,000 teacher-written examples.
  • The result: a model that fits on one GPU with most of its memory left for users' conversations, so many more people are served on the same hardware, while keeping much of the teacher's skill on the tasks it was shown.
  • The catch: the big teacher still has to be trained first, and the student only learns what the teacher demonstrates.
A smaller model lets one GPU do more for the same power: more users, less waiting on data.
Source: DeepSeek-AI, “DeepSeek-R1,” arXiv:2501.12948, 2025. Probabilities shown are illustrative.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Smaller models, 3: mixture of experts
A huge model whose effective size, for each word, is small
One word
(a token)
Router
scores all 384 experts, keeps the top 8
384 experts, each a small feed-forward network · 8 used for this word
Output
weighted sum
32B of 1Tweights used per word in Kimi K2 (3.2%)
~31× lessmath per word than a dense model of the same size
  • Kimi K2 has 384 experts in each layer; the router sends each word to 8 of them, plus 1 shared expert that every word uses.
  • The catch: all 1 trillion weights still sit in GPU memory, so mixture of experts saves math, not memory.
Each word runs a 32B model, not a 1T one, so one GPU does more for the same power.
Source: Moonshot AI, Kimi K2 README (8 of 384 experts active per token; 32B of 1T parameters).

Research changes the curve: linear attention
Optimization makes today's method cheaper. A new method changes how the cost grows.
full attention (n²)Kimi Linear hybrid (3:1)linear attention (n)rest of the model
FLOPs to read the whole context (y axis, log scale)
Reading 1 million tokens, one H100 at peak
Full attention1.4 × 10¹⁸≈ 23 min
Kimi Linear hybrid3.4 × 10¹⁷≈ 6 min
Linear attention4.7 × 10¹⁴≈ 0.5 s
Rest of the model6.7 × 10¹⁶≈ 68 s
Kimi Linear (Moonshot AI, Oct. 2025)A new attention, Kimi Delta Attention, keeps a fixed-size memory instead of looking back at every token. Three of these layers for every full-attention layer gave up to 75% less KV cache and up to 6× faster decoding at 1M tokens, while beating full attention in the authors' tests.
Optimization moves you along the curve; research changes the curve. At long contexts, n² → n beats every other trick.
Source: Kimi Team, “Kimi Linear: An expressive, efficient attention architecture,” arXiv:2510.26692, 2025. FLOP counts are our estimates for a Kimi K2-sized model (61 layers, 64 heads, head sizes 192/128, 128 × 128 linear state per head, 32B active), causal prefill; time at the H100's 989 TFLOPS dense BF16 peak.

What to take away
Talk it over with a neighbour before we move on
?
  • An AI data center is GPUs, CPUs, storage and network, nested chip → server → rack → cluster → campus, and every layer is sized in watts.
  • GPUs draw more power because they do far more math per second, not because they are wasteful.
  • Every watt becomes heat, and moving data over distance is the expensive part.
  • Water use depends on the cooling design on site and the grid's power sources off site.
  • Inference gets cheaper through engineering (batching, caching, quantization, distillation, experts), and fastest through new ideas like linear attention.
Five years from now, which will have cut the cost of AI the most: better chips, better engineering of today's models, or new ideas in the models themselves? Why?

Check the facts

Chips and racks

~74 billion operations per word (Kimi K2): 2 × 32B active weights + attention 61 layers × 64 heads × 2 × (192 + 128) × 4,096 words; 99.9% are matrix multiplies

7,168 multiply-adds per output: Kimi K2's hidden size

CPU peak 7.2 TFLOPS: 56 cores × 2.0 GHz × 64 operations per cycle

GPU 9× to 138× faster, 4.7× to 69× per joule: 67 or 989 TFLOPS vs. 7.2; then ÷ 700 W vs. ÷ 350 W

GPU rack ≈ 15× average rack: 120 kW ÷ 8 kW

+80 vs. +2 TWh: Gartner 2026 minus 2025 (175 − 95; 195 − 193)

Power, heat, water

Memory read ≈ 170× a multiply: 640 pJ ÷ 3.7 pJ

PUE overhead: 100 kW × (1.09 − 1) = 9 kW; × (1.56 − 1) = 56 kW

87 space heaters: 130 kW ÷ 1.5 kW

Electricity slice: 176 ÷ 3,874 TWh = 4.5%; AI servers 40 ÷ 3,874 ≈ 1%; commercial 1,408 − 176

Litres per kWh: NREL gal/MWh × 3.785 ÷ 1,000 (e.g. nuclear tower 672 → 2.5)

100 MW site for a day: 100,000 kW × 24 h = 2.4 million kWh; × 1.9 L = 4.6 million L; × 2.54 L = 6.1 million L

Once-through withdrawal ~170 L/kWh: 44,350 gal/MWh × 3.785 ÷ 1,000

Water slice: 66 billion L ÷ (322 Bgal/d × 365 × 3.785) = 0.015%; AI ≈ 40 ÷ 100 of that; indirect 4.5% × 133 ÷ 322 ≈ 1.9%

Cheaper inference

295 operations per byte: 989 TFLOPS ÷ 3.35 TB/s

Math units busy: (2 × batch operations ÷ 2 bytes) ÷ 295, capped at 100%

Energy per operation: 320 pJ ÷ (2 × batch) + 0.75 pJ → 161 pJ at batch 1, 1.1 at 512 (~150×)

Caching, 750× less work: 1,001 + 1,002 + … + 2,000 = 1,500,500 passes vs. 2,000

KV cache 70 KB per token: (512 + 64) × 2 bytes × 61 layers; × 131,072 tokens = 9.2 GB

Quantized weights: 10¹² × bits ÷ 8 = 2 / 1 / 0.5 TB; users = (1,440 GB − weights) ÷ 9.2 GB → 47 and 102

Distillation: 37 ÷ 7 ≈ 5× less math; 671 ÷ 7 ≈ 96× less memory

Mixture of experts: 1T ÷ 32B ≈ 31× less math per word

Linear attention: full = 61 × 64 × 320 × n²; linear = 61 × 64 × 7 × 128² × n; rest = 2 × 32B × n; time = operations ÷ 989 TFLOPS; crossover at 2 × 32B ÷ (61 × 64 × 320) ≈ 51k tokens

Debatable or uncertain

Hydro ≈ 0 water: NREL counts reservoir evaporation (~17 L/kWh). We don't charge it: the fair comparison, the same land with no dam, isn't a real option. Others do charge it.

Energy figures are from a 2014, 45 nm chip; today's are lower. The 640 pJ read is only confirmed as "over 500."

Estimates simplify: batching ignores attention reads; linear-attention cost is a rough model; server overhead is ignored.

Industry totals (Gartner, IEA, Synergy) use different methods; prices change monthly.

Water pie mixes 2015 national withdrawals with 2023 data-center use; AI's water share is estimated from its power share.

Sources are in the slides. Numbers are estimates.
